system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2138-06-26 18:14:00 to 2138-06-29 17:19:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for post-procedural monitoring and pain management following a flexible bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and left main stem bronchus due to recurrent airway stenosis from relapsing polychondritis and Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome. The procedure successfully dilated the airways and removed obstructive pseudomembrane and granulation tissue. He experienced moderate chest pain managed with oxycodone and reported epigastric pain attributed to pirfenidone, which was addressed by increasing famotidine to twice daily. His white blood cell count rose post-procedure but was deemed reactive. He remained stable, with mild atelectasis on chest X-ray resolving clinically. He was discharged home with a short course of prednisone, instructions to continue all home medications, and follow-up planned with pulmonology.
problems: Long term (current) use of systemic steroids
Elevated white blood cell count, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your doctors here. I understand you had trouble breathing earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I suddenly couldn’t catch my breath and turned blue. I called ___ and they sent an ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That must have been scary. You were given oxygen and breathing treatments at the other hospital, and your breathing improved. We’re keeping you here to monitor you and figure out what caused this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. It’s because of the narrowing in my airway from my condition. I have that Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. Those conditions can cause scarring and narrowing in your trachea and bronchi. Your oxygen level was low when you arrived, so we’ve put you on extra oxygen through your trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That feels better already. But will I need another balloon procedure again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for that. Interventional pulmonology will see you tomorrow and likely do a bronchoscopy to check the airway and possibly dilate it again if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I remember that from last time. It helped, but it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can be recurrent. We’ll manage it step by step. We also checked your blood, and your white blood cell count is high, which can happen with inflammation or infection, but we don’t think it’s an infection right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a fever or cough. Could it be from my steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Chronic steroid use can raise your white count. We’ll watch it. Your chest X-ray didn’t show pneumonia, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your bronchoscopy schedule — it’s set for 12 PM today. The team will look into your airway and open any tight spots with a balloon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep? I was awake last time and it was uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under sedation this time, so you’ll be comfortable. Afterward, we’ll keep you here for monitoring and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my potassium was high yesterday — is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was slightly high on admission but came down. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s not concerning now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. How are you feeling after the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but my breathing feels easier already. Was it successful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They found significant narrowing in your trachea and both main bronchi. They used balloons to open them up — your left main stem and trachea were dilated successfully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might be worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also took some washings from your airway to check for infection. Results aren’t back yet, but we’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been using my tobramycin nebulizer. I didn’t have a nebulizer at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that’s important. You have chronic Pseudomonas colonization, and that nebulizer helps keep your lungs clear. Infectious disease recommends restarting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it was that important. Can I get a nebulizer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send one home with you, along with the tobramycin prescription. It’s key to preventing flare-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll use it. What about my Esbriet? I stopped that too — it was giving me stomach upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your GERD symptoms may be from Esbriet. We’ve kept your famotidine twice daily, which should help. Please restart Esbriet with meals — it’s important for your lung health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. And my chest pain — is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG showed some changes, but they look chronic — not new heart damage. Your troponins were negative. It’s likely related to your connective tissue disease, not your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I only take oxycodone occasionally for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it available for pain. You’re on 10 mg every 6 hours as needed, and it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better. Your white count has dropped from 18 to 8.9 — that’s a good sign of reduced inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. And my breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on room air now through your trach mask and saturating at 100%. No more desaturations. The bronchoscopy really helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We want to make sure you’re stable and have all your prescriptions ready, especially the nebulizer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’re clearing you for discharge today. Your breathing is stable, labs are good, and you’re feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications — especially the tobramycin nebulizer and Esbriet with food. Use the oxycodone only if you have pain. And follow up with pulmonology in one month for another bronchoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start having trouble breathing again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER. We’ve also given you a Narcan spray in case of accidental overdose — keep it handy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you — I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — the bronchial washings. What if they find something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still pending, but even so, we’re continuing the tobramycin because of your history. If anything urgent comes up, your doctor will call you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you have your nebulizer, medications, and follow-up appointments scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s here. I’ll start the nebulizer tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And remember, your condition needs consistent care. Staying on your meds helps prevent these hospital visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll do better with adherence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update — your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll get my things together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check — any chest pain or breathing issues since this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None. I feel steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re doing well. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your rheumatology follow-up is scheduled. Keep taking your prednisone and losartan as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll see you all in a month.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure due to recurrent tracheal and bronchial stenosis from Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome and relapsing polychondritis. He presented with sudden shortness of breath and cyanosis at home, requiring EMS transport. He was stabilized with oxygen and nebulizers, then underwent bronchoscopy with balloon dilation of the trachea and bilateral mainstem bronchi, which improved his airway patency and oxygenation. His leukocytosis resolved without antibiotics, and pain was managed with oxycodone. He was restarted on home medications, including tobramycin nebulizers and Esbriet, with a new nebulizer provided. He was discharged home with follow-up planned in one month for repeat bronchoscopy and continued management of chronic conditions.
